analysis.one_liner: Lets consumers opt out of online tracking of their browsing and personal data.
analysis.headline: The Do Not Track Me Online Act, backed by Rep. Jackie Speier and 22 Democratic cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Federal Trade Commission to write rules giving internet users a simple way to opt out of having their online activity tracked and collected by companies. It covered browsing history, location, unique identifiers like IP addresses, and sensitive data such as health, financial, and religious information. It also required companies to disclose their data practices, let the FTC audit compliance, and gave state attorneys general power to sue violators for penalties up to $5 million per series of violations. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat without action until the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, who today have their browsing habits, location, and personal details collected and sold largely without meaningful control. The bill would have given them a one-click opt-out, disclosure of who gets their data, and enforcement by the FTC and state attorneys general.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FTC to set standards for an online opt-out mechanism so consumers can easily prohibit companies from collecting or using their online activity, identifiers, and personal information.
Requires covered companies to clearly disclose what data they collect, how they use it, and whom they share it with.
Covers sensitive categories including medical history, race, religion, sexual orientation, financial records, precise geolocation, biometric data, and Social Security numbers.

Lets state attorneys general sue violators for civil penalties up to $11,000 per day of noncompliance, capped at $5 million per related series of violations, and preserves stronger state privacy laws.
Directs the FTC to conduct random audits of covered companies and report publicly at least once a year on consumer-privacy risks.

analysis.who_pays: Online advertisers, data brokers, and website operators whose business models depend on tracking users across the internet to sell targeted advertising. Compliance costs and opt-outs would shrink the pool of trackable users they can monetize.

drawbacks.text: The bill relied on FTC rulemaking with broad exemptive authority, so final rules could have carved out large categories of 'commonly accepted commercial practices' such as analytics and product improvement, weakening the practical protection.
It offered an opt-out rather than an opt-in, meaning tracking would remain the default and consumers had to actively find and use the mechanism to be protected.

Small companies were exempt: businesses storing data on fewer than 15,000 people or collecting from fewer than 10,000 per year, or not tracking as their primary business, were not covered, leaving gaps in protection.

Critics of do-not-track proposals argued the rules would reduce advertising revenue that funds free online content and impose compliance costs, though this objection came from the industry the bill would regulate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — giving consumers real control over who tracks them online and what happens to sensitive data — is substantial and the mechanism was achievable through existing FTC authority. The weaknesses are real but ordinary: reliance on opt-out rather than opt-in, room for the FTC to write broad exemptions, and coverage gaps for smaller firms. On balance the bill would have shifted power over personal data from companies to individuals at modest cost to the tracking industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, which never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, so it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Jackie Speier introduced the bill on February 11, 2011, with Reps. Alcee Hastings and Bob Filner as original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, and a week later to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade.
All 22 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill expired with the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online advertisers, data brokers, and companies whose revenue depends on tracking users across the web kept an unregulated field. Consumers gained nothing and remain without a federal do-not-track right.

for.name: Rep. Jackie Speier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Do Not Track Me Online Act and sought an FTC do-not-track rule.

for.name: 22 Democratic House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican joined.

for.name: Consumer and privacy advocates
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed do-not-track legislation during the 2011-2012 debate over online privacy, keeping pressure on Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Fred Upton (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade
against.what_they_did: Took jurisdiction on February 18, 2011, and never acted on the bill.

against.name: Online advertising and data-broker industry
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against mandatory do-not-track legislation and promoted self-regulation instead during the 2011-2012 privacy debate.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Democratic — Speier and 22 Democratic cosponsors, no Republicans — and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Their revenue depends on tracking users across sites and selling profiles; a consumer opt-out would directly shrink the data they can collect and monetize. The bill would have given consumers a legal right they currently lack.

They would lose some targeted-ad revenue if users opt out, but the bill exempted ordinary service-provision and analytics uses, and small operators under 15,000 stored records were excluded entirely. Many would face compliance costs while keeping most current practices.
